title: Summarize Various Types of Attacks and Their Impact to the Network

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Network attacks target availability, switching, address resolution, DNS, wireless access, network services, people, and endpoints.
bullets: Rogue DHCP, rogue APs, evil twins, and on-path attacks
Phishing, dumpster diving, shoulder surfing, and tailgating
sections.callout: OVERWHELM → BYPASS → IMPERSONATE → REDIRECT → INTERCEPT → DECEIVE → INFECT

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When network behavior becomes abnormal, identify whether an attacker is exhausting resources, bypassing segmentation, corrupting mappings, redirecting DNS, introducing rogue infrastructure, intercepting traffic, manipulating people, or deploying malware.
bullets: Fake MAC entries fill a switch table → MAC flooding

sections.title: Denial-of-Service Attacks

entries.title: Denial-of-Service (DoS)
paragraphs: A DoS attack makes a system, network, or service unavailable by exhausting bandwidth, CPU, memory, connection capacity, or application resources, commonly from one primary source.

entries.title: Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS)
paragraphs: A DDoS attack coordinates many systems against one target, making source blocking more difficult while producing the same availability impact.

sections.callout: One source → DoS. Many distributed sources → DDoS.

entries.title: VLAN Hopping
paragraphs: VLAN hopping attempts to bypass segmentation and reach traffic or resources on another VLAN.

entries.title: Media Access Control (MAC) Flooding
paragraphs: MAC flooding overwhelms a switch's address table with fake source MAC entries, disrupting normal forwarding and potentially causing less-secure traffic handling.

sections.title: ARP Poisoning and Spoofing
paragraphs: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps local IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses. Manipulated mappings can redirect traffic.

entries.title: ARP Poisoning
paragraphs: ARP poisoning is the corrupted result: hosts store false IP-to-MAC mappings.

entries.title: ARP Spoofing
paragraphs: ARP spoofing is the action of sending forged ARP messages while impersonating another system.

sections.callout: Forged message → Spoofing. Corrupted mapping table → Poisoning.

sections.title: DNS Poisoning and Spoofing

entries.title: DNS Poisoning
paragraphs: DNS poisoning corrupts resolution information or a DNS cache so users receive maliciously incorrect answers.

entries.title: DNS Spoofing
paragraphs: DNS spoofing sends a falsified response that impersonates legitimate DNS information.

sections.callout: Fake response → Spoofing. Corrupted stored resolution data → Poisoning.

sections.title: Rogue Devices, Evil Twins, and On-Path Attacks

entries.title: Rogue DHCP
paragraphs: An unauthorized DHCP service gives clients malicious or incorrect addressing, gateway, or DNS settings.
entries.memoryHook: A fake address server gives bad directions.

entries.title: Rogue AP
paragraphs: A rogue access point is an unauthorized wireless device connected to or operating inside an organization, creating an uncontrolled network path.

entries.title: Evil Twin
paragraphs: An evil twin deliberately imitates a trusted WLAN's SSID, appearance, or login experience to attract victims.

entries.title: On-Path Attack
paragraphs: An on-path attacker secretly positions between communicating endpoints to observe or manipulate their traffic while both believe they communicate directly.
entries.memoryHook: The attacker sits in the middle.

sections.callout: Any unauthorized AP → Rogue AP. An AP impersonating a trusted WLAN → Evil twin. Interception of an existing path → On-path.

sections.title: Social Engineering
paragraphs: Social engineering attacks people rather than relying only on technical exploitation.

entries.title: Phishing
paragraphs: Deceptive messages trick users into revealing credentials or sensitive data, sending money, or executing malware.

entries.title: Dumpster Diving
paragraphs: Attackers search discarded materials for passwords, diagrams, account data, labels, or other useful information.

entries.title: Shoulder Surfing
paragraphs: An attacker observes someone entering or viewing a password, PIN, or other secret.

entries.title: Tailgating
paragraphs: An unauthorized person follows an authorized person through a controlled entrance into a restricted area.

sections.title: Malware
paragraphs: Malware is malicious software designed to damage, disrupt, spy on, control, steal from, or further compromise systems. Network impacts include propagation, data theft, outages, and unauthorized control.
sections.callout: Harmful software executing on an endpoint → Malware.

entries.title: DoS vs. DDoS
paragraphs: One source → DoS. Many distributed sources → DDoS.

entries.title: VLAN Hopping vs. MAC Flooding
paragraphs: Reach another VLAN → VLAN hopping. Overload the MAC table → MAC flooding.

entries.title: ARP Poisoning vs. ARP Spoofing
paragraphs: Corrupted mapping table → Poisoning. Forged ARP messages → Spoofing.

entries.title: DNS Poisoning vs. DNS Spoofing
paragraphs: Corrupted DNS information → Poisoning. Fake DNS response → Spoofing.

entries.title: Rogue DHCP vs. Rogue AP
paragraphs: Unauthorized address service → Rogue DHCP. Unauthorized wireless device → Rogue AP.

entries.title: Rogue AP vs. Evil Twin
paragraphs: Unauthorized AP → Rogue AP. AP deliberately imitating a trusted WLAN → Evil twin.

entries.title: Evil Twin vs. On-Path
paragraphs: Fake WLAN attracts the victim → Evil twin. Attacker intercepts an existing communication path → On-path.

entries.title: Phishing vs. Shoulder Surfing
paragraphs: Deceptive message → Phishing. Physical observation → Shoulder surfing.

entries.title: Dumpster Diving vs. Tailgating
paragraphs: Search discarded materials → Dumpster diving. Follow someone through an access point → Tailgating.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
sections.callout: OVERWHELM → BYPASS → IMPERSONATE → REDIRECT → INTERCEPT → DECEIVE → INFECT
